before: The 4th-person A prefix shows a dialectal split within the left personal layer. Saru and the western dialects use a= exclusively; Tokachi, Ishikari, Shiranuka, and Samani favour an= under locally varying conditions, and Nakagawa takes an= to be the older form . Both shapes occupy the same left-edge position ‹consensus›.
after:
The basic 4th-person A prefix varies between a= and an=. Saru and varieties farther west normally use a=. Nakagawa nevertheless records apparent an= forms in Saru, Chitose, and Horobetsu, especially in formulaic verse. He interprets these as survivals of an older form .

In Tokachi, an= occurs before vowel-initial words whose accent is not on the first syllable; a= occurs elsewhere. Nakagawa reports no conditioning of the alternation in Shizunai. Ishikari, Shiranuka, and Samani usually have an=, with a= also attested; Shiranuka particularly favours a= with ye 'say' .
evidence: Nakagawa2024:168–169, original image169 inspected. Ordinary western a= admits verse exceptions; Tokachi has phonological/accent conditioning; Shizunai differs.

before: <S t="The right personal layer: =as and =an" id="right-layer">
after:
The A and O inventories do not combine uniformly. In Saru and Chitose, eci= covers all four first-person A to second-person O number combinations. A second-person singular A acting on first-person O is marked by en= (1SG.O) or un= (1PL.O), without a separate e=. Chitose uses the same bare forms for a second-person plural A; Saru has eci=en= and eci=un= in those cells .

Other dialects include combinations with a suffix on a transitive verb. Horobetsu has e=…=as for first-person singular or plural A acting on 2SG.O. Ishikari distinguishes singular e=…=an from plural e=…=as in that relation, with es= replacing e= for 2PL.O . The suffix therefore does not by itself identify an intransitive predicate or a fixed person value across dialects.

The first-to-second-person combinations are compared in .

before: The portmanteau character of the 1→2 form is confirmed by the contrast with the 1→4 combination. Nakagawa's Saru combination table records eci=i= when the agent is first person and the object is fourth person: the agent index eci= and the fourth-person object i= appear as separate prefixes . The 1→2 cells merge the two slots into one, in keeping with the two-index cap: a verb carries at most one agent index and one object index, and the portmanteau satisfies both positions simultaneously. The cap and its consequences for three-argument verbs are treated in .
after:
Saru also has combinations with two overt prefixes. Nakagawa records ku=i= for 1SG.A→4.O and eci=i= for 2PL.A→4.O; the latter contains the ordinary second-person plural eci=. His 1PL.A→4.O cell is a=i= . The single eci= of the 1→2 cells therefore has to be distinguished from eci= as one member of a longer prefix sequence. Object-indexing restrictions are treated in .

The 1→2 forms differ elsewhere in Hokkaido. Horobetsu has e=…=as or eci=…=as, according to object number. Ishikari uses e=…=an and es=…=an with a singular A, and e=…=as and es=…=as with a plural A. Tokachi has eci=…=an across all four number combinations . These combinations are illustrated in .
